If knowledge meant being free of matter, and this meant being known, then saying that Zayd knows the sun would mean that the sun is free of matter for Zayd but not for Amr. If it meant being the knower, then Zayd would be free of matter in relation to the sun but Amr would not. This is not what “free of matter” means. Nor does it follow that the sun's image is free of matter, since this account says knowledge is freedom from matter itself, not a mental image.

The author first objects that knowledge cannot be an image if knowing ourselves is simply our self. A second, broader problem concerns anyone who says that an immaterial being's knowledge of itself is identical with its own being. The answer is that the rejected “image” means the essence by which a thing is what it is. In that sense, knowing ourselves can be our very self. But what can be understood as an image is not identical with the real existence that is knowledge itself. On the author's view, the real existence of knowledge is known only through direct awareness.
When he later explains his preferred view, the author will say that this further positive state is the luminous existence of the essence.

One might ask why this view is attributed only to the author of Al-Mulakhkhaṣ. Many philosophers say that knowledge is a quality and also has a relation to what is known. The difference is that the author seems to make it just a quality, like a mere likeness. The philosophers combine the quality with an image of the essence itself. The author objects to keeping essences in the mind as qualities; he returns to this below.
Suhrawardi may mean a relation of illumination. If so, the objection does not apply, because a free existence that takes the form of an image is itself an illumination and a relation.

The stronger objection is that, on Suhrawardi's view, bodies are dark in themselves, while knowledge must be light to itself or light to something else. The reply is that bodies, though dark, are lit by the Light of Lights. In this way they become light to something else—not as things that receive light, but as things that give it.
A relation exists only in the mind, and only as a dependent kind of existence. It is not an independent object that can match or fail to match another thing, as an idea can.

One might ask how this applies to simple ignorance, where there is no mental image. There are three replies. First, the author's own explanation applies. Second, confused ignorance is a kind of knowledge, so it can be said of an image. Third, ordinary reasoning would place the relation in the case where some kind of knowledge is present, even if it is false. Why, then, could that relation not be knowledge?
The objection confuses two meanings of “ignorance” and two meanings of “knowledge.” It assumes that ignorance always means simply not knowing.

This point supports the author's view. Just as direct knowledge of an immaterial thing is evidence against treating knowledge as a relation, this example also shows that knowledge need not be a relation.

Once knowledge has been defined as existence free of matter and position, this objection no longer applies. It is also answered by what the author says about the image account, so it may be better to omit it.

The image can be like the thing, so this explanation should be read in light of the clearer one. By “image,” the author means either the essence itself, which he has already rejected, or an essence existing as light. He means the latter.

That is, knowledge is possible only through direct awareness. This occurs when a thing knows itself or what comes from it. A human being may know the reality of existence in this first way by becoming absorbed in it.

The objection is tied to the author's view because, if knowledge is an immaterial existence and our souls are immaterial existences, then our knowledge of ourselves would be our own existence, as he says.
If one thing is joined to another, and that second thing is joined to a third, the first and third are joined too.

This leads to two problems: a simple, unified self would have to contain many complex forms, and there would be an endless chain of knowledge about knowledge. Both problems are clearer if essences, rather than existence, are taken as the basic reality, since each concept would then be a separate thing.

If our awareness that we know ourselves is not the same as our knowledge of ourselves, and knowledge is different from what is known, then our knowledge of ourselves cannot be the same as our self either.

On this answer, our knowledge that we know, and each further level of knowledge, is our self in reality but different in the way the mind considers it. The chain stops when the mind stops considering another level.
The answer does stop the endless chain, but it does not answer the worry about one simple, unified self containing many forms and combinations.

Al-Tusi seems to mean that direct awareness of ourselves is our own individual existence. It is different from our self only as a concept: the concept “knowledge of self” is not the same as the existence of the self. This brings his answer back to the one the author approves.

Direct awareness of ourselves exists as our own being. But our learned idea of ourselves—for example, that our soul is an immaterial substance that governs the body, or that it began with the body or existed before it—is not the same as our being. The author's answer is better because al-Tusi's works for direct knowledge.
That is, acquired knowledge that knowledge is a quality of the soul, or has some other nature. In short, it is knowledge of what knowledge is.

Al-Tusi's account of the sense organ is not the point at issue. Both authors agree that an individual image is present. They disagree on two things. First, others say the image seen exists in the sense organ; the author says it is produced by the rational soul in its lower activity. Second, others say the image seen flows from the First Emanator, while the author says it flows from the soul. He explains this elsewhere.

The point is that material bodies hide some of their parts from one another. Their existence therefore includes the possibility of nonexistence: the whole is not fully present to each part, nor each part to the whole. But for a perceiver to know something, the whole thing must be present to it. Material substances and their features cannot be known as they exist in matter. Put another way, a physical image cannot itself be a mental image. This could be shown more clearly by starting from the body's motion within its substance: mental images are certainly present to us, but the parts of a moving material thing are not all present together. So mental images must exist free of matter. This argument also avoids some wording objections.

What has no unity cannot be one thing with another, so it cannot exist. One might object that a continuous whole has a single unity. But can its parts and whole really be one and the same? For a claim to be true of both, the parts must not be separated in position. The parts of a continuous whole do not meet that condition, even though they are connected in existence.
This is especially true when we think of a body as extending and changing through time. Substantial motion makes it more potential and increases its nonexistence.

Material qualities crowd each other out within one subject. Mental images do not: the soul is one, simple, and without size, so it can receive them all. The concepts represented by those images can still conflict in any kind of existence.

The soul's ability to receive all forms at once depends on its being free of matter. This also underlies the teaching about bodily resurrection: the soul has no size, so it has no parts of its own, and it can hold the five kinds of sensory images together at one time. It may imagine heat or cold, a taste and a smell, while also seeing and hearing. It can hold opposite images together too, such as black and white, or loud and quiet. In this way the soul shows that nothing keeps God from attending to many things at once.

“Position” here means the category of place, not any arrangement within an image. The imagined body of Zayd may have its limbs in order, but the image itself has no position as a material thing. As we have said, an imagined length cannot actually be divided; if we imagine half of a forearm, the mind makes a new half rather than uncovering two existing parts.
This refers to the intellectual image. The understood reality is the thing stripped of its material distinctions. It is one and the same whether it is known by one intellect or a thousand.

Each person is a complete world and does not need the contents of another person's world. The same is true of the life to come: each believer's paradise is as wide as the heavens and the earth, not only in length but in every direction.
That is, this holds when the image is an accident, not a natural form.
This difference concerns a divinely supported soul. In its direct knowledge of itself, its image is already complete and it can develop by its own resources, like the souls of the heavenly spheres.

This is true of general ideas. Particular images are said of their objects in the ordinary, concrete sense. Directly imagined images are like what is directly sensed, as we explained when discussing mental existence.

This view seems more useful than the account in the current book. It says, for example, that an intellect understands a substance as a substance by its definition, not by being that kind of substance in the ordinary sense. But this can make it seem that the intellectual image has no real substance, much like the idea of an impossible partner to God. The author will soon clarify that intellectual realities are higher than substance, not lower. The soul, on this view, has no separate essence of its own, and is not simply an accident either. This question may be resolved either through the unity of knower and known, or through the view that universals are known by seeing their separate exemplars, the immaterial intellects. Suhrawardi, for example, says that these intellects have no essences.

At first glance, mental existence seems to be a state in which the thing's outside effects do not occur. So we affirm the idea in its own terms and deny it of the mental image in the ordinary, concrete sense. On closer inspection, however, the mental image is an imaginal or intellectual form: it is more complete than material existence and has effects suited to its own level. It seems to have no effects only when we compare it with the material effects. This is a difference between levels of stronger and weaker existence. The form may be said to be both the same as and different from its material counterpart, depending on whether we mean their shared reality or their different levels.
“Kind” here means a level of existence, not a species. The imaginal and intellectual images share the same species in essence as their material examples, but exist at a different level.

“Substance” applies when something is actual and does not depend on a subject, even as a possibility. This is like a body, which can have three intersecting lines even when no lines are drawn in it, as in a sphere.

“Meanings” here refers to the world of meanings, including the divine realm and the separate intellects. Rumi says: “Generations passed, one after another; those meanings remain, enduring.” Every reality has a meaning and a form, a deeper reality and its outward appearance, a root and its branch. Its root is present in the soul. After God and the completely separate intellects, the soul is simple in its reality, and a simple reality gathers within itself, in a higher way, the existences beneath it. When the soul wants to know something, it turns to the page of its own being, where the form of that thing is already present. By “form” I mean what makes a thing actual.

As explained earlier, a reality in the soul can both be affirmed and denied of it: we deny its material boundaries and imperfections, which are absent from the soul's single, simple existence; we affirm it because its higher existence is the root and source of the material thing. Thus when the author says that the understood animal includes the understood body, growth and sensation, he means that the soul gathers these meanings in a higher, simpler existence. The soul knows itself directly, rather than through a separate image residing in it. That is why the difficulties about how a mental image could itself be a substance, grow, sense or move do not arise in the same way once the knower and what is known are understood as one. The same applies to bodily extension: the soul contains bodily existence in a higher manner, without sharing its limits. A fine verse puts it this way:
“O you who are a complete copy of the divine book, and a mirror of the King's beauty: nothing in the world is outside you. Seek within yourself whatever you desire—for you are that.”

It is not right to deny these realities of this all-embracing existence, which is a reflected unity. In natural existence, one human being contains the powers of matter, plant life, and animal life. More generally, being does not have to belong to one thing only. Concepts such as existence, unity, identity, and light can be true of many things. An essence and its defining features can also exist in a broader reality. These ideas are all present together in the higher, intellectual existence.

By “animal,” Avicenna means the natural kind of animal; he actually uses the example of a human being. The intellectual universal in the author’s earlier discussion has another meaning. Al-Tusi also understands Avicenna’s words as referring to the natural universal, as is clear to anyone who reads the beginning of the fourth section of The Pointers. The intellectual universal is not without the natural universal.

The point is that an accident is not just a description that can be added to something; it is a kind of existence that depends on a subject. To exist in a subject is the way qualities such as blackness and heat exist. Existence itself does not truly attach to an essence as another feature. The mind separates them in thought. So an essence's existence is not like a passing feature that can change while the essence remains. A substance could not keep the same essence while its very way of existing changed from depending on a subject to not depending on one. Comparing existence with other incidental features is not a sound comparison. Existence is not truly added to an essence; it is the thing's being real. More exactly, each kind of existence must suit the essence that exists: an accident exists in a subject, and a substance exists on its own.

The truth, as we have explained elsewhere, is that knowledge is not a quality, as al-Dawwānī says. It is the existence that the soul spreads over all the essences present in the intellect, imagination, and common sense. It is the soul's light shining on the forms that receive it, just as God's light shines on all things in the worlds of intellect, soul, and matter. God's giving existence is not itself a substance or an accident; likewise, the soul's light is neither substance nor accident in itself. It takes the nature of the things it illuminates. This view is more satisfying than al-Dawwānī's, because for him knowledge belongs to the same category as what is known.
The proof appears later, in the discussion of how intellect is intelligible to itself and understands itself.

The claim rests on a broader principle: when something exists for another, its existence in itself is the same existence it has for that other. This applies to accidents and their subjects, forms and matter, and—if a cause and its effect have direct awareness of one another—to causes and effects. If we consider a dependent existence apart from what it belongs to, we must also consider the thing that owns it. If that existence can stand on its own, then owner and owned are one thing at the same level, as when a substance exists in itself or an immaterial soul knows itself. Otherwise, the dependent existence belongs at a level within the existence of what it depends on, as a dependent being belongs within the being that supports it. This shows that an accident is a level of its substance’s existence, matter and form are one in existence, and an effect is a level of its cause’s existence (and a cause, in turn, is a higher level of its effect). But this principle does not prove that knower and known have one existence at the same level. The commentator therefore rejects the claim that an understood form can be intelligible in act whether or not any intellect understands it: we cannot set the form apart from its knower, even by placing it at a higher level. He also points out that a relation between knower and known is a real opposition between two sides, which cannot belong to one thing in one and the same respect.

In short, an object of thought in itself and in act has no feature or aspect other than being understood; being understood is its very existence. It remains intelligible even if we set everything else aside, because its existence is luminous and aware. Although we form the idea of “being understood” by reference to an intellect, setting the intellect aside also sets aside the object’s existence as understood. If its existence remained, it would still be something and still be intelligible, which would contradict the claim that it had no intellect. One might object that an effect is essentially an effect, and so would have to be its own cause. The reply is that being an effect is essential to the effect in the sense that it needs no further feature in order to be called an effect; it still needs a distinct cause. An intelligible form, by contrast, can be understood without another intellect, as in the case of the Necessary Being.

The point is not that, because knower and known are related and matched in level, either one must be found wherever the other is found—including in the other’s own essence. Their being matched means they exist together, not that one has the same existence as the other. The author’s point is that the actual knower corresponding to an actual object of thought cannot be a separate soul that contains it as a vessel contains something. If the soul were the knower while remaining separate from the known form, then it would be only potentially a knower of it. When the form is understood in act, the form itself is what knows it. This is a second proof, distinct from the earlier proof that an actual object of thought has no existence apart from its luminous intellectual existence. If the first proof does not rely on the general rule about related things, how do we know that there is a knower at all? We rely on the principle that the known form’s existence in itself is its existence for the knower—not on the general logical category of relation. The form’s being understood in itself does not prove that it is joined to another thing by such a relation. The author later allows an illuminative relation: the understood form depends on the soul for its existence, and the soul depends on it in turn.

To truly possess something is to have it in one’s own being, not merely to stand in a relation to it. A person who only “has” something in a secondary sense still lacks it in their own being; their possession is only a relation. Existence itself belongs truly to existence, not to an essence that becomes real by receiving existence as an extra feature. In the same way, knowledge truly belongs to the intellectual form itself; the form is knowledge because it is what is known.

“What is other than the image” means things outside the mind. They may be called objects of thought in themselves because their images are present to the knower. The images, however, are mirrors through which attention sees the things; they are not always what attention is directly fixed on. If every image had to be understood by means of another image, the process would go on forever.
Unless these things are levels and aspects of your own existence.

The proof given here treats the presence of an understood form to its knower, the presence of an impressed image to matter, and the presence of an accident to its subject as cases of one kind: a dependent feature exists within what it describes. The subject does not stand outside the existence of that feature; it is found within the feature’s range of existence. The same applies to direct awareness between cause and effect. The knower and known may exist at one level, as when the soul knows itself; or one may be a level within the other’s existence, as when an effect knows its cause or a cause knows its effect. On the author’s account, all direct knowledge falls into these cases. But this does not mean that knower and known must exist at exactly the same level. If they did, we could not know accidents, which would then have to exist in themselves, or know a cause and its effect without making them equal in rank. Think carefully about this distinction.

Here we have the beginning of a proof that the knower and what is known become one, as Alexander argued. This is particularly clear if, as the author and al-Sayyid al-Sanad maintain, matter and form make one being, rather than two things merely joined. The soul is like matter and what it perceives is like its form. If matter and form have this kind of union even among physical things, how much more is it possible in understanding? A subject and an added quality, by contrast, are united only in a different, more limited sense.

By union we mean being one in existence, not having the same meaning. The various things understood have different meanings, and their meanings differ from that of the knower; yet their existence can be one. Otherwise the intellect would consist merely of concepts, like the independent essences assumed by the Muʿtazilites. When we speak of clearly distinguished forms of knowledge, they are one with the knower as the knower becomes manifest, not with the hidden depth of the knower's being. But the simple, all-embracing intellect, which contains knowledge without separate parts, can be one with that hidden depth. The higher unity contains many within one, and detail within what is undivided; detailed knowledge displays unity within multiplicity. This distinction between levels is needed if we are not to collapse all forms of existence into one undifferentiated thing.

There are other proofs. First, what the intellect understands is free of matter, and everything free of matter understands itself. If it is objected that an understood form depends on something else, as an image supposedly depends on the soul, I deny that such forms exist merely by being housed in another: the universal forms of substances are substances, and an essential feature cannot cease to be essential. Even the claim that imagined images reside inside something has been challenged; it is still less suitable for intellectual forms.

Second, we have explained that understanding universals is a way of witnessing the separate intellects. Earlier philosophers also held that the intellect receives such knowledge from them. Definitions and proofs point in this direction, and the soul stands in a direct relation of awareness to these intellects. They are themselves capable of understanding.

Third, the real bearer of a description is the reality from which that description comes. Existence itself is what truly exists, and whiteness itself is what is truly white; in the same way, knowledge is the true knower. The philosophers call the soul an intellect in possibility when its understood form is still possible, and an intellect in actuality when that form is actual. Thus it is an intellect, or a knower, through what it understands.

Fourth, the soul in the higher depth of its being gives rise to the distinct forms it understands. What gives existence and completeness cannot be wholly without them; it must possess them in a higher way. This reasoning applies whether their source is the simple intellect, the inward depth of the soul, or the Active Intellect.

Fifth, the outward world and the world of the mind correspond, like twins nourished with the same milk. To say that Zayd exists outside the mind is to place him within a level of the outward world. In the same way, what is understood exists at a level of the soul and its powers: the mind is not a container holding mental objects. Together with the opening argument from matter and form, these make six proofs. Insight also supports them. As Rumi says: “Brother, you are thought itself; the rest is bone and sinew.”

This argument assumes the common view that an accident has an existence separate from the existence of its subject. On the more accurate view, which the author supports elsewhere, an accident is a level of its subject’s existence. The issue is then like the union of knower and known.

Avicenna argues that if a form could receive another form, it would have to change into something else, and the forms would not be incompatible. The commentator objects that this argument is refuted by the all-embracing existence that flows from God: it is one, yet united with many different possible essences, such as the essence of a human being, which has no capacity to receive the essence of a horse and does not turn into one. The key is that this all-embracing existence has no single, fixed boundary; it has degrees, from stronger to weaker. The rational soul is like this too: its unity is a reflected unity. If Avicenna insists that every existence joined to one essence must be wholly separate from every existence joined to another essence, then the essences themselves would have to be simple, separate existences. This leads to serious problems, including the famous doubt attributed to Ibn Kammūna, and would leave no real unity. The commentator therefore reads the differences among such existences as differences in the essences they manifest, not as divisions in existence itself.

This happens in the immaterial soul. The soul can prepare itself through acts of thought and receive divine or angelic thoughts as lights from the Active Intellect. When it understands absolute, simple existence, or recognizes itself as life, universal light, knowledge, will, and love, its existence turns toward these perfections. It does not take on their self-standing existence; it joins them through a dependent, intellectual illumination, whether near or far. The soul then grows and becomes one with these perfections in the way described earlier.

The commentator distinguishes the soul’s essence from its existence. Perfections are added to the soul’s essence, but not to its existence. In the separate intellects, knowledge, will, and power are their existence, so no further perfection is waiting for them. These perfections are still “added” to their essence in the sense that an essence, considered on its own, is only what it is.

The passage refers to one continuous individual of motion, extending from its beginning to its end. A changing quality has three possible kinds of individual: one is a single, continuous, time-stretched individual, from rest to rest; another consists of the portions that the mind can distinguish within that duration; a third is a series of supposed instants, each with a separate individual before and after it. The first is one individual with different degrees of completeness and existence, and can support different concepts as it changes.
“Matter” here means what something depends on or is attached to. It does not have to mean bodily prime matter.

In the beginning, the soul was the specific form of a bodily being. It was like a sensory or imagined form, but less fully actual, because the soul can undergo growth and change while those forms resist it. This potential for development, despite its weakness, is far better than being fixed in a fully actual state. The commentator notes that Avicenna’s objection is about an intelligible form, while the author’s reply first speaks of a specific bodily form. The reply still addresses the point behind Avicenna’s objection: before it understands anything, the soul is already a form, and Avicenna says a form cannot receive another form.

Strictly speaking, this kind of growth is not “receiving” a new form. It is a weaker existence being absorbed into a stronger one as it grows. If “receiving” is used here, it means that the soul comes to be described by a further perfection. Even if one grants that an actual form cannot receive another actual form, that does not undermine the union of knower and known, because that union does not depend on such reception.

The first kind of potentiality is accompanied by the thing’s actual absence from the outside world, as when one form replaces another. The second belongs to growth toward a higher level: the thing exists, but its expected perfection does not yet exist. If we compare it with what comes later, that absence is in thought; if we compare it with what came earlier, what is absent is its earlier lack or incompleteness. The second kind is not an external absence in the thing itself.

The author’s phrase “a form connected to matter” means that the form can grow because it is attached to matter; considered simply as a form, it cannot receive another form or change. Through its relation to bodily matter, the soul can grow from intellect in act toward the Active Intellect and beyond. Imaginal forms that have no matter cannot develop in this way. That is why the afterlife is not a place where the soul continues to grow, even though what it sees and understands may become clearer over time. The world is the field where the soul grows; the afterlife is where it gathers what it has cultivated. As the saying goes, wheat grows from wheat and barley from barley. The clearest answer is that an essence cannot receive another essence; only existence becomes stronger or weaker. The body’s matter supplies the receptive capacity for this growth.

The intelligible forms are manifestations of the soul’s own being, not its hidden essence. Their appearing existence is the soul’s existence as it shines outward; they do not move away from the soul or diminish it.

The true intellect in act is the understood form, not the soul as the subject in which that form is found. The soul remains potentially intelligible to itself until that form appears. The author elsewhere answers the objection that the soul is already an intellect and intelligible to itself before it knows other things by saying that even its self-awareness is only potential—imagined or not yet fully clear.

Avicenna does not mean that the soul’s bare self, with no relation to intelligible forms, is the knower. He means the soul as related to the forms it understands: the relation is within the knower, while what it understands is outside it.

The point is that an intellectual form is an intellect in itself, even if Avicenna says the soul is an intellect because of that form. The form is intellect for itself; it is not intellect merely for the bare soul that receives it.

The Active Intellect exists in itself and also exists for us. Our souls become one with the way it exists for us, not with its own existence in itself. Its existence for us has endlessly many levels, though its own being is one. The multiplicity lies in how it appears. So it does not follow that a soul must understand everything the Active Intellect understands, or that every soul joined to it must know everything known by every other soul joined to it.

The claim is not that many separate existences literally turn into one, which would be impossible. Nor is it that their existences remain separate but count as one because they are copies or reflections of a single thing; that would be unity in multiplicity. The point is multiplicity gathered within unity: one simple intellectual existence is the higher mode of all the things understood, and contains them within its unity as its manifestations and aspects.

This is a formal argument: pure existence is pure being, and nothing that is pure has any distinction mixed into it. If we suppose two instances of pure whiteness, they must differ by their subjects, their times, or something else. Then neither is pure whiteness alone; each includes something beyond whiteness. The same argument applies to pure existence. The intellectual meaning of pure existence or whiteness is therefore one and the same wherever it is understood, whether by Zayd or by the Active Intellect; the two do not have separate copies of it. Otherwise, we would have to ask what universal meaning they share, and the same problem would continue without end. The commentator compares this to radiating lines that meet at one center. The direct awareness each soul has of itself is likewise one in meaning once incidental features are set aside.

Intellectual unity is a true, reflected unity, not numerical unity. If the soul becomes one with one aspect of an all-embracing intellect, it does not follow that it becomes one with every other aspect. A single intellect can have many inherent aspects. The soul itself is knowledge, power, will, and love in its own way, yet it does not consciously know all of these simply by knowing itself. Likewise, knowing the divine does not mean knowing every feature of the divine being.

The commentator offers a different reading from the author’s. He thinks “different movements of life” refers to differences in bodily movement and temperament. He also takes movements of intellect to include acts of thought. He says the author’s reading—“movement” as outflow from different causal aspects such as necessity and possibility—fits differences in kinds of effects better than differences among individual intellects. The separate human soul, for example, is said to come from one source in the Active Intellect; individual differences arise from the mixtures and readiness of bodies.

The claim is that the intellect that is the special source for the horse cannot also be the special source for the human being. It does not mean that a human being cannot understand a horse. Separate intellects do not block one another from knowledge: each knows God, and knowledge of a cause entails knowledge of its effect.

There are two possible readings of “when the First Intellect understands something, it and what it understands are one.” It could mean that the First Intellect understands the universal forms of the kinds beneath it; that would support the author’s claim about the unity of knower and understood form. Or it could mean that the First Intellect understands its own highest reality and, in that direct self-knowledge, knows its lower manifestations. On the second reading the passage would not prove union with something other than itself. The statement that it understands nothing for which it has no intellect means that a passing individual thing is not its knowledge: otherwise its knowledge would change as that individual thing passed away.

The commentator takes this passage to support his own view that kinds and their intellectual forms come from separate intellects at the same level—the intellects that serve as lords of those kinds. The higher and lower causal aspects mentioned by the author act as preparatory causes; they do not directly produce the species. Differences in rank within the same level come from how one kind relates to its own lord and to the lords of other kinds.

Each intellect that serves as the lord of a particular kind has its own rank and care. The intellect that serves the horse is not the intellect that serves the cow. “The first intellects,” by contrast, includes the separate intellects both in the vertical chain of causes and among the lords of kinds.

The commentator questions the author’s decision to identify “universal life” only with the natural universal and “universal intellect” only with its intellectual form. Both terms can be used at both levels. The point is to distinguish the natural universal, the intellectual universal, and the actual separate intellect. They are different in how we consider them, yet united in existence as reality and manifestation, essence and being. The example is not simply that one universal meaning is found in many individuals; it concerns a wider intellectual existence that contains and gives rise to them.

I say: this takes a needlessly long route. It would be better to say that the intellect that comes to be is a manifestation of the separate intellect corresponding to its kind, its lord. A thing’s manifestation is its appearance, and in one respect that appearance is the thing itself. The lord of a kind is like its spirit and the kind like its body, so there is a kind of union between them. Here “coming to be” is contrasted with “being brought forth”: the soul begins with the body, or through the body’s coming to be. It does not mean the “is” that connects the parts of a statement. Nor is the intellect that comes to be deprived of its separate intellectual source, for it depends upon it at first and becomes one with it in the end.

“Parts” may mean intellectual manifestations of the whole, such as the perfected intellects of divinely guided people, or the meaningful parts of an understood animal: its understood head, hand, and foot. This reading fits the author’s purpose of showing that the soul can unite with the universal intellect.

The commentator considers al-Rāzī’s account very weak. How could a bare relation exist within one simple, immaterial being? The difference between “knower” and “known” is a difference in what is predicated of a thing, not necessarily a difference in the thing that bears those descriptions. Al-Rāzī’s strongest reply is that the knower must turn its attention toward itself or toward an image of something else, and that this attention is a relation. The commentator answers that attention is itself awareness, so the explanation cannot show that awareness is only a relation. Every act of knowing something else also includes awareness of oneself. If knowledge remained only when the knower also knew that it knew, then awareness of awareness would be needed in turn, without end.

“Relation” by itself is too broad a category. It needs distinguishing features before it becomes a specific kind of relation. One might, for instance, describe knowledge as a relation between different sides, not involving bodily position, through which something is disclosed. A surface likewise is not simply quantity in general, but a continuous, fixed quantity extending in length and breadth. The critic has not proved even that knowledge is a relation in the broad sense; he has only asserted it. He points to some conditions for a relation, such as the existence of both sides, and tries to remove objections concerning self-knowledge or knowledge of what does not exist. That is a serious failure of explanation: it would have been better not to attempt the argument.
Al-Rāzī accepts that the difference between the two descriptions is only a difference in meaning.

Calling these careful investigators “literal-minded” and their words “grand poetry” invites us, in turn, to call this imam a crafty opponent, scheming and conceited. If they were really literal-minded, people content with surface meanings would understand and approve their words, and would not join you in attacking them. Since the opposite is plainly the case, be fair: this is an exalted question, difficult to reach.

Al-Rāzī means that the subject described by both attributes is one and the same, but that the attributes themselves differ in essence and existence. He treats them as separate features added to the subject, like knowledge and will in a human being.

The commentator finds this objection weak. If it worked, any two ideas that always go together in thought would have to be one and the same idea. Al-Rāzī answers this point, but the commentator thinks the question was different: whether the same subject can truly bear both descriptions, not whether the descriptions have the same meaning.
This refers to the familiar argument that two identical things cannot exist together in the same place.

The proof should have divided the possibilities more carefully: if the relation exists, the conclusion follows; if what is present is only a matching image, or something different that is related to the thing, the same conclusion must be examined. Al-Rāzī’s argument does not cover every case it needs to address.
That is, a reversal in the wording of the two propositions.

For example, fatherhood and sonhood arise through a particular seed and the placement and arrangement of the people involved. The commentator says al-Rāzī’s account of knowledge as a relation has no comparable positive basis. On the philosophers’ account, the intellectual image itself is the positive feature that corresponds in essence to what is known.
As in the case of the Necessary Being.

The objection divides perception into only two kinds and leaves out an immaterial being’s knowledge of itself. That is a mistake. As the author says, knowledge is a luminous, representational existence. It includes an immaterial being’s presence to itself, since it is not hidden by matter, time, space, or other coverings.

This makes explicit the earlier argument that a thing’s being understood is one case of its existing for something. An immaterial thing’s existence for itself is its knowledge of itself; its existence for another is that other thing’s knowledge of it. The knower cannot be outside the existence of what it knows. There is a qualification: dividing existence into existence for itself and existence for another seems to make the two mutually exclusive. That would mean an immaterial substance, which exists for itself, could never be understood by another. The exception is when they stand in a cause-and-effect relation: each then has a kind of existence for the other.

What the author says about relations is the clear truth implied by their nature. A relation is a kind of opposition, and its two sides cannot coincide in the very respect that defines the relation. This is how we should read scattered passages that seem to say the two sides may coincide unless some outside cause prevents it, though some of the author’s statements appear to resist this reading.
